subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

options: The increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the growth in the share of a population living in urban areas.

questions.q: A 'push factor' encouraging rural-urban migration is:
options: Lack of jobs or services in rural areas
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from an area; pull factors attract them to another.
Pull factors such as jobs, services and housing attract migrants to cities.

questions.q: A megacity is usually defined as a city with a population of over:
questions.explain: Megacities have more than 10 million inhabitants.

questions.q: Rapid urban growth in lower-income countries often leads to:
questions.explain: Fast growth can outpace housing and services, creating informal settlements.

questions.q: A challenge of informal settlements is:
options: Poor sanitation, services and housing quality
questions.explain: Informal settlements often lack clean water, sanitation and secure housing.

questions.q: 'Suburbanisation' is the movement of people and activities:
options: From the inner city to the outer edges of the city
questions.explain: Suburbanisation expands cities outward as people seek space and cheaper housing.

questions.q: A city building better housing, transport and services to improve life for slum residents is carrying out:
questions.explain: Improving informal areas and regenerating urban districts raises quality of life.

options: The movement of people from cities to rural areas
questions.explain: Counter-urbanisation sees people leave cities for the countryside, often aided by remote working.

options: Younger people leave rural areas for work, leaving an ageing population
questions.explain: Out-migration of young people leaves declining, ageing rural communities.

questions.q: A 'commuter (dormitory) village' is one where residents:
options: Live in the village but travel to a town/city for work
questions.explain: Commuter villages house people who work elsewhere, changing rural character.

questions.q: Second-home ownership in rural areas can:
options: Raise house prices, making them unaffordable for locals
questions.explain: Second homes can price out local residents and leave villages quiet off-season.

questions.q: Improved transport links between rural and urban areas can:
options: Allow commuting and bring services, but also increase pressure on the countryside
questions.explain: Better links create interdependence but can cause development pressure.

questions.q: The area of older housing and industry around a city centre is often called the:
questions.explain: The inner city surrounds the CBD and often faces regeneration challenges.

questions.q: A village gaining wealthy commuters but losing its shop and school shows that rural change can be:
options: Both positive and negative for different groups
questions.explain: Rural change brings investment but can erode local services and community.

questions.q: Rural and urban areas are 'interdependent' because:
options: They rely on each other for food, jobs, services and resources
Cities produce all their own food
questions.explain: Urban and rural areas are linked through flows of people, goods and services.
